text: Every real program eventually hits an error, and every platform here has its own way of catching one. T-SQL's try-catch, PL/SQL's exception block, MySQL's handler model, and Postgres's own exception block all solve the same problem, but one of them, MySQL, is genuinely more awkward than the rest — and that's worth understanding clearly, not just memorizing.

T-SQL's version is covered in depth elsewhere in this catalog's T-SQL course, so just a quick reminder here. Begin try, select one slash zero, end try, begin catch, print error message open paren close paren, end catch. One generic catch block, and error message and error number give you the details inside it.

PL/SQL goes further by letting you catch specific named exceptions before falling back to a catch-all. Begin, select list price into v underscore price from products where product id equals ninety-nine nine nine nine, exception, when no data found then put line no product found, when others then put line sqlerrm concatenated with sqlcode. No data found and too many rows are real, specific, built-in Oracle exceptions — and sqlerrm and sqlcode give you the message and numeric code inside any handler.

MySQL is where things get genuinely more awkward, and it's worth naming honestly. Declare v underscore price decimal, declare exit handler for sqlexception, begin, select an error occurred, end, then your actual select statement comes after, completely separate from the handler. There's no single block you wrap the risky code in — the handler is declared ahead of time, disconnected from the code it's protecting, and plenty of developers find that genuinely less intuitive than try-catch or an exception block.

PostgreSQL's PL slash pgsql, once again, tracks Oracle closely. Begin, select list price into v underscore price from products where product id equals ninety-nine nine nine nine, exception, when no data found then raise notice no product found, when others then raise notice percent comma sqlerrm, end. Named conditions, a catch-all, and sqlerrm for the message — nearly a direct match for PL/SQL's model.

So: T-SQL's generic try-catch, PL/SQL's and Postgres's named exceptions with a catch-all, and MySQL's separately-declared handler, which is the real outlier in ergonomics here. Next lesson, triggers — including a genuinely important difference between T-SQL's set-based inserted and deleted tables and Oracle's row-by-row colon-new and colon-old references. See you there.
